scenes.title: Flexible Endoscope Reprocessing
scenes.narration: Flexible endoscope reprocessing. These instruments are semi-critical, heat-labile and mechanically complex, and they are the source of the most serious documented outbreaks.

Flexible endoscopes are heat-labile, so they cannot be steam sterilised. High-level disinfection is the usual process, and its margin is smaller than that of sterilisation. Their narrow channels differ between models, and some are easy to forget. In use they are heavily soiled with organic material; biofilm forms readily and, once established, resists chemical disinfection entirely. They are expensive, so hospitals own few and turnaround is under constant pressure. And they are fragile: damage admits fluid into the interior, where it cannot be cleaned.
rows: High-level disinfection is the usual process
Differ by model; some easy to forget
Biofilm forms and resists chemicals entirely
Damage admits fluid that cannot be cleaned

scenes.narration: Reprocessing follows a defined sequence. It starts with the bedside pre-clean, immediately after the procedure. Next is the leak test, before the scope is immersed. Manual cleaning follows, then high-level disinfection. Last come rinsing, drying and storage.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Bedside pre-clean]:::red --> B[Leak test] --> C[Manual cleaning] --> D[High-level disinfection] --> E[Rinse, dry, store]:::teal

scenes.narration: The bedside pre-clean comes immediately after the procedure, before the scope leaves the room. Organic material begins to dry and form biofilm within minutes, and no later step reliably removes it. It is done by the busiest person at the busiest moment, so it is often abbreviated. The leak test comes before immersion, every time. A breach lets fluid into the interior, where organisms multiply, and the scope is irreparably contaminated. The test takes a minute, and it is skipped when the list runs late.
rows: Bedside pre-clean, before the scope leaves the room
Biofilm forms within minutes; no later step removes it
Leak test, before immersion, every time
Fluid enters; scope irreparably contaminated inside
Takes a minute; skipped when the list runs late

scenes.narration: Manual cleaning begins with full immersion in the correct detergent, at the correct dilution and temperature. Wipe the exterior and the insertion tube. Then brush every channel to the manufacturer's instructions for that model, with a brush of the correct diameter and length, until it emerges visibly clean. Brush the ports, valves and elevator recess as well. Flush all channels with detergent, then water, using the connectors specified for that model. Remove, clean and disinfect or replace the removable parts, which are frequently forgotten. Finally, inspect for damage and residual soil.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Immerse in detergent] --> B[Wipe exterior and insertion tube] --> C[Brush every channel until clean]:::red --> D[Brush ports, valves, elevator recess] --> E[Flush with detergent, then water] --> F[Clean removable parts] --> G[Inspect for damage and soil]:::teal

scenes.narration: Brushing is the only step that removes biofilm. Chemical disinfection does not penetrate an established biofilm. Soaking does not remove it. Flushing does not remove it. Only mechanical action, with a brush that physically contacts the channel wall, disrupts it. That is why brushing is specified for each channel, why brush diameter matters, and why omitting it has repeatedly caused outbreaks.
rows: Yes: contact with the channel wall disrupts it

notes.note: Brushing is specified for each channel
Omitting brushing has repeatedly caused outbreaks

scenes.narration: Usually in an automated endoscope reprocessor, every channel must be connected to the correct connector for that model. An unconnected channel is not perfused and is not disinfected. The agent must reach the correct concentration, temperature and contact time, and the solution is discarded at expiry regardless of the test result. Rinse with water of defined quality, since residual disinfectant causes chemical colitis and mucosal injury. Dry with an alcohol flush where protocol specifies, then forced air through every channel. Residual moisture lets Pseudomonas multiply between uses. Store hanging vertically and uncoiled, with valves removed, in a controlled drying cabinet.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Connect every channel] --> B[Correct connector for the model] --> C[Concentration, temperature, time] --> D[Rinse with defined-quality water] --> E[Dry: alcohol flush, then forced air] --> F[Store hanging vertically, uncoiled]:::teal

notes.note: Residual moisture lets Pseudomonas multiply between uses

scenes.narration: Duodenoscopes have an elevator mechanism at the distal tip, which directs accessories. Its recess is narrow, mechanically complex and extremely difficult to clean. It has been implicated in multiple international outbreaks of multidrug-resistant organisms in patients with no other common exposure. Where you use duodenoscopes, follow the manufacturer's instructions for the elevator exactly, and keep in place any additional measures the manufacturer or infection control specify.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Elevator at the distal tip] --> B[Narrow recess, extremely hard to clean] --> C[Multidrug-resistant outbreaks]:::red --> D[Follow manufacturer instructions]:::teal

scenes.narration: For every procedure, record the scope, the patient, the reprocessing cycle and the operator. Where a transmission is suspected, this is the only means of investigation. The defined response is to quarantine the scope, review the records, involve infection control and microbiology, and consider patient notification. Scopes are also sampled microbiologically at defined intervals, with quarantine and reprocessing after a positive result.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Scope] --> B[Patient] --> C[Reprocessing cycle] --> D[Operator] --> E[Quarantine the scope]:::red --> F[Review records, infection control]:::blue --> G[Consider patient notification]:::teal

notes.note: Traceability is the only means of investigating a transmission
Microbiological surveillance at defined intervals per protocol

scenes.narration: Scopes are expensive, lists are long, and turnaround determines throughput. The resulting pressure underlies most of these failures. When a list is late and one scope is available, a technician under direct pressure decides whether brushing was adequate. That decision should not rest on individual courage. It needs written policy and a defined right to hold the scope back, with adequate inventory, staffing and visible management backing.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
 A[Expensive scopes, long lists] --> B[Sustained time pressure] --> C[Technician judges brushing alone]:::red --> D[Written policy, right to hold back]:::teal --> E[Inventory, staffing, management backing]:::teal

notes.note: Reminding technicians to be thorough does not resolve it

scenes.narration: To summarise. The pre-clean and the leak test cannot be omitted, because biofilm and internal contamination cannot reliably be undone later. Brushing is the only step that removes biofilm. And the pressure of turnaround is met with written policy, adequate inventory and management backing, not individual courage.

notes.note: Never omit the pre-clean or the leak test
Brushing is the only step that removes biofilm
Written policy, inventory, backing: not courage
